segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Phil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I'm Beth.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: So, Beth, we're talking about the best education systems in the world today.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: You went to school here in Britain. What do you think of the British education system? Do you think it could be the best?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I think that it's quite good. There's probably a couple of things that I personally would change

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: about it, but I would say it's quite good, but maybe not the best in the world.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Well, in this programme, we're going to be talking about the PISA rankings.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: The rankings are based on tests carried out by the OECD, that's an international organisation,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: every three years. The tests attempt to show which countries are the most effective at teaching maths,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: science and reading. But is that really possible to measure? Well, here is former BBC education

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: correspondent Sean Coughlin talking to BBC World Service programme The Global Story.

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: When they were introduced first of all, that was a very contentious idea because people said,

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: how can you possibly compare big countries, how can you compare America to Luxembourg or to,

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: you know, to parts of China or whatever?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Sean said that the tests were contentious.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If something is contentious then it something that people might argue about It controversial So at first PISA tests were contentious because not everyone believed it was fair to compare very different countries

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Phil I got a question for you about them

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So in 2022, Singapore was top of the reading rankings.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But which of these countries came second?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Was it A, the USA, B, Ireland or C, the UK?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I think it might be B, Ireland.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK, well, we will find out if that's correct at the end of the programme.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A common pattern in the PISA rankings is that the most successful countries tend to be smaller.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Talking to BBC World Service programme The Global Story,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Sean Cochland tells us that many large countries from Western Europe don't score that highly in the rankings.

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: They're being outpaced and outperformed by these fast upcoming countries, Singapore or Estonia or Taiwan or those sort of places, which we don't historically think of as being economic rivals.

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: But I suppose the argument for the PISA test is if you want to have a knowledge economy, an economy based on skills, this is how you measure it.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: We heard that many large European countries are being outpaced by smaller nations.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If someone outpaces you, they're going faster than you, at a higher pace.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: We use the prefix out to say that someone or something is better at doing something.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: We also heard that smaller nations are outperforming larger ones They performing better Singapore Estonia and Taiwan are described as economic rivals to large European nations That means that they are competing with them

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: economically.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: We also heard about a knowledge economy. This is an economy based on service

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: industries that require workers to be highly educated, such as IT, finance or advanced

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: engineering.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So what makes countries perform better in these tests? Let's hear again from BBC

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: World Service programme The Global Story. Sean Coughlin tells us that those countries that

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: prioritise getting everyone to a certain level do well. We also hear from Rando Kustik, an Estonian

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: school principal.

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: Countries which make sure that all their pupils get through a certain level of

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: education to a certain standard, regardless of their background, do well.

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: If you are teaching them by different level of abilities, then you are segregating them.

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: And we don't want to segregate any people in the world. Why we are doing that in the schools?

segments.speaker: Sean Coughlan
segments.text: This is one of the main things why the Estonia is successful.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Sean said the most successful systems educate everyone to a particular standard, regardless

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: of their background. If one thing happens regardless of something else, it means that

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: the something else is not important or not a problem

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Rando Kustik said that Estonian schools do not want to segregate students Segregate means to separate and keep apart

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: So we just heard about Estonia but what about your question Beth What about those countries

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I asked you which out of the USA, Ireland and the UK came second for reading in the 2022 PISA rankings.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: You said Ireland and that was the correct answer. Well done.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learnt in this programme about education rankings,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: starting with contentious, argued about or controversial.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If you're outpaced by someone, they're going faster than you are.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Rivals are competitors.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: A knowledge economy is one based on industries that need highly educated workers,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: such as IT, finance or advanced engineering.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: If something happens regardless of a second thing,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: the second thing has no impact on it happening.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And finally, if people are segregated,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: different groups of people are separated and kept apart.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Remember to visit our website, bbclearningenglish.com,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: where you'll find a worksheet and quiz related to this programme.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and we'll see you again soon for more trending topics

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and useful vocabulary here at 6 Minute English.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Goodbye for now.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Bye.
